ABSTRACT
We report a previously unidentified issue with model-free, value-
based approaches to multiobjective reinforcement learning in the
context of environments with stochastic state transitions. An ex-
ample multiobjective Markov Decision Process (MOMDP) is used
to demonstrate that under such conditions these approaches may
be unable to discover the policy which maximises the Scalarised
Expected Return, and in fact may converge to a Pareto-dominated
solution. We discuss several alternative methods which may be
more suitable for maximising SER in MOMDPs with stochastic
transitions.
KEYWORDS
multiobjective reinforcement learning, multiobjective MDPs, sto-
chastic MDPs
1 INTRODUCTION
Multiobjective reinforcement learning (MORL) aims to extend the
capabilities of reinforcement learning (RL) methods to enable them
to work for problems with multiple, conflicting objectives [ 12].
RL algorithms generally assume that the environment is a Markov
Decision Process (MDP) in which the agent is provided with a scalar
reward after each action, and must aim to learn the policy which
maximises the long-term return based on those rewards. In contrast
MORL algorithms operate within multiobjective MDPs (MOMDPs),
in which the reward terms are vectors, with each element in the
vector corresponding to a different objective. This creates a number
of new issues to be addressed by the MORL agent. Most notably
there may be multiple policies which may be optimal (in terms of
Pareto optimality), and which policy the agent should learn is not
immediately obvious.
In the utility-based paradigm of MORL [12, 29] it is assumed that
the preferences of the user can be defined in terms of a parame-
terised utility function f , and that the aim of the agent should be to
learn the policy which produces vector returns which maximises
the utility to the user as defined by f .
Various approaches have been explored for the form of the utility
function – some may be better suited to express the preference of
the user within a particular problem domain, while others offer
benefits from an al

6 CONCLUSION
We have described a stochastic MOMDP and utility function which,
despite their seeming simplicity, are not amenable to solution by the
widely-used model-free value-based approaches to MORL. While
this issue with MOMDPs with stochastic state transitions has pre-
viously been described in the context of probabilistic planning [2],
this is the first work to identify the implications for MORL. Our
example also demonstrates that under stochastic state-transitions,
it is in fact possible for such MORL methods to converge to a Pareto-
dominated policy.
The combination of SER optimisation, stochastic state transi-
tions and the need for a deterministic policy are likely to arise
in a range of applications (particularly in risk-aware agents), and
so awareness of the limitations of some MORL methods to work
under these characteristics is important in order to avoid the use
of inappropriate methods.

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=Can+falsification+of+core+reward-scalarization+assumptions+be+automated+in+reinforcement+learning+architectures%3F&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6836287\", \"title\": [\"Research on Trajectory Planning for Automated Vehicles Based on Reinforcement Learning in Sparse Reward Environments\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Trajectory planning for automated vehicles in complex and dynamic environments is the core issue of automated driving systems. Dynamic obstacles and nonlinear road conditions in complicated traffic scenarios pose severe challenges to the stability and adaptability of planning algorithms. Meanwhile, reinforcement learning fails to converge efficiently under sparse reward conditions, resulting in low learning efficiency and unstable trajectories. To solve the above problems, this paper proposes a reinforcement learning-based trajectory planning model for automated vehicles, namely the Intrinsic Curiosity Module–Progress Hindsight Experience Replay (ICM-PHER). This model introduces an intrinsic reward mechanism driven by prediction error to facilitate effective exploration, thereby alleviating training inefficiency caused by sparse rewards. Combined with curriculum learning, a dynamic target point guidance strategy is designed to enable vehicles to learn gradually from simple tasks to complex ones. Furthermore, an improved Hindsight Experience Replay (HER) mechanism integrated with a dynamic filtering sampler is adopted to remove low-quality experiences and improve the utilization efficiency of valid samples. A multi-scenario automated driving simulation platform is established to verify the performance of the proposed model. Experimental results show that compared with baseline methods, the ICM-PHER model delivers up to 300% higher average reward in sparse reward and complex scenarios, reduces training collisions by about 60%, and increases key indicators including speed and trajectory length by 23%–230%. The proposed method greatly boosts exploration efficiency and trajectory planning performance, and effectively improves the trajectory planning efficiency and complex environment adaptability of automated vehicles in sparse reward settings.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6836287\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.20944/preprints202610.1802.v1\", \"title\": [\"Automated Dense Reward Function Design for Reinforcement Learning in Autonomous Driving\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Crafting reward functions remains a challenge in reinforcement learning, particularly in autonomous driving (AD), where safety, efficiency, and task completion must be balanced. We introduce a GPT-5.6-based revision of AD Reward Designer, a framework for generating interpretable dense reward functions from natural language goals and concise Pythonic environment descriptions. The initial reward generation requires no expert demonstrations or model fine-tuning. GPT-5.6 translates task requirements into executable reward code, which is checked before being used by a reinforcement learning algorithm. Policy rollout summaries and human feedback then guide iterative refinement of the reward terms and their weights. An optional demonstration-conditioned extension supplies expert and policy trajectories as additional context for reward design. We retain Highway-env and MetaDrive as the evaluation environments and PPO as the policy learning algorithm. The original experiments provide evidence for the feasibility of language-model-generated rewards; their numerical results are retained as historical evidence and are not reported as GPT-5.6 measurements. The revised GPT-5.6 configuration requires a new evaluation under the same task settings.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202610.1802.v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 10, 20]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.4024901\", \"title\": [\"Reward Is Not Enough: Can We Liberate AI From the Reinforcement Learning Paradigm?\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>I present arguments against the hypothesis put forward by Silver, Singh, Precup, and Sutton: reward maximization is not enough to explain many activities associated with natural and artificial intelligence including knowledge, learning, perception, social intelligence, evolution, language, generalisation and imitation. <br><br>I show such reductio ad lucrum has its intellectual origins in the political economy of Homo economicus and substantially overlaps with the radical version of behaviourism. <br><br>I show why the reinforcement learning paradigm, despite its demonstrable usefulness in some practical application, is an incomplete framework for intelligence -- natural and artificial.<br><br>Complexities of intelligent behaviour are not simply second-order complications on top of reward maximisation.
